newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bonn, Paris must air EMU differences-Kohl aide.
newsitem.headline: Bonn, Paris must air EMU differences-Kohl aide.

text.p: A senior associate of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Tuesday that the leaders of France and Germany must meet soon to clear up differences on the planned single European currency and economic policy.

Karl Lamers, European policy spokesman of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told Reuters in an interview that it was urgent for French and German leaders to have a fundamental discussion to get to the bottom of their differences.

"On many of the issues on which we have differed or still differ today, there has never been a deep enough dialogue," he said. "This is not the first difference between the Germans and the French...we have differed in the past on foreign policy, for example on relations with America."

Lamers welcomed the fact that new French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin had for the first time spoken of the need to reduce public deficits this year, calling it the first sign that the left-wing government in Paris was taking the Maastricht treaty criterion of limiting deficits seriously.

Kohl pledged on Tuesday that Germany would meet the strict 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP goal on time in contrast to French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, who said last week that Paris would definitely not make the target.

Lamers said he was convinced Paris would come round to making a further effort to cut its deficit because it was clear that a failure to launch the European economic and monetary union (EMU) would have terrible consequences for France.
"I never said it was important to reach exactly 3.0 percent. There can be unforseen factors that get in the way. But governments must display clear determination to achieve this goal," he said.

"The worst thing that could possibly happen for France and for all other member states, would be a failure. And that's why (France) will definitely not allow itself to be a cause of failure," he said.
The German aide said Jospin would have less time than his predecessors to realise that there was no alternative policy to fiscal orthodoxy.

"I said before the French elections that when the Socialists came to power in 1981, it took Francois Mitterrand two years to realise there was no other policy, it took (current President) Jacques Chirac half a year. Lionel Jospin won't have that much time," he said.
Lamers played down the importance of opposition in Germany, notably in the right-wing Bavarian government, to starting the single currency on time.

Asked whether he was sure that launching EMU was politically feasible in Germany, he said: "It is achievable. I have no doubt about that, whatever (Bavarian state premier Erwin) Stoiber says. This will be decided in Europe and in Bonn."
Lamers clashed with French Socialist party leader Francois Hollande at a day-long conference in Paris on problems in Franco-German relations.
Holland accused Bonn of distorting the purpose of EMU by stressing the strictest reading of the criteria to the exclusion of economic policies to promote growth and jobs.
"We diverge only on the question of the right economic policy to overcome unemployment, not on the aim of fighting this scourge," Lamers said in the interview.
